It is mouse cells in mouse embryos, with no human cells and no organ grown across species, so it does not meet the animal rung. Nothing else dated 2026-11-02 to 2026-11-09 was found in the trial registry, the paper index, company releases or the press.

findings.what: Ding, Oura, Okamura and Wu, "Epiblast complementation enables generation of live offspring from pluripotent stem cells", Cell Stem Cell, peer-reviewed. The abstract says donor mouse stem cells replaced the whole embryo proper in host mouse embryos and gave live offspring, and that the older method "has largely been limited to individual organs". Same species throughout; no human cells; abstract read on Europe PMC, full text not opened.

records.found: Nothing in the window reaches the first-human rung: no trial of a treatment that removes or resets age-biased blood stem cells in people was posted, and no report in a person appeared. Two items in the window bear on the animal work: a preprint posted 2026-11-02 reporting restored production of immune cells and a better vaccine response in aged mice by a different route (calming a group of brain cells that signal to the marrow), and a peer-reviewed mouse paper in Blood dated 2026-11-05 describing a group of blood-forming cells that keeps its lymph-cell output in old age. A registry entry updated 2026-11-04 shows a placebo-controlled trial in people aged 60 and over with a blood-cancer precursor condition, not yet recruiting, aimed at restoring normal blood production; it was first posted 2026-02-27 and the records do not hold it.

findings.what: Preprint (Research Square, not peer reviewed), Jin and colleagues, "Targeting the inflamed paraventricular hypothalamic-bone marrow axis rejuvenates lymphopoiesis in aged mice": the abstract reports that switching off an over-active group of brain cells in aged mice restored early lymph-cell precursors and B-cell production in the marrow and improved the response to an H1N1 flu vaccine. A second route to the animal rung the record already holds; mice only.

Peer-reviewed paper in Blood, Romero-Mulero and colleagues, "Multimodal omics identifies a lymphoid-biased multipotent progenitor population with limited age-associated remodeling": in mice, one group of blood-forming cells kept its long-term lymph-cell output in old age while the stem cells themselves shifted toward the inflammatory side; the authors call it a possible target for restoring balance. A description, not a treatment.

Registry entry NCT07435636 (the MOSAIC trial; sponsor Clinical Hub for Interventional Research, Australia) updated: phase 2, placebo-controlled, 80 people aged 60 and over with a blood-cancer precursor condition (clonal cytopenia), not yet recruiting, start expected 2026-12-01, main results expected 2030-12. Its stated goal is to restore normal blood cell production; its main measure is the share of mutated blood cells at 24 weeks, not immune age. First posted 2026-02-27. It is the kind of condition the estimate names as the likely way into people, though the drug is a low-dose existing medicine, not an antibody that removes cells.

records.found: In the window: Vertex said on 2026-11-02 (results release) and 2026-11-03 (quarterly filing) that it "has decided to focus on accelerating the development of VX-017", a second islet cell therapy for all blood types, in place of zimislecel, and expects VX-017 to enter its deciding trials in 2027; neither document mentions a filing for approval of zimislecel. That pushes the diabetes route to an approval later than the record assumes. Separately, and outside the window, the record lacks a larger fact: on 2026-03-06 Japan's health ministry gave a conditional, time-limited approval to Amchepry, a Parkinson's cell therapy grown from donor stem cells (Sumitomo Pharma), which on a plain reading may already meet the clinic rung; the author should rule on whether a conditional approval counts.

findings.what: Vertex third-quarter 2026 results release (filed copy): "Given the rapid progress with VX-017, Vertex has decided to focus on accelerating the development of VX-017, which has the potential to reach more patients than zimislecel, which is designed for patients with blood types A or A/B only. Vertex expects to advance VX-017 into pivotal development in 2027." VX-017 is in an early (phase 1/2) trial and has the United States regulator's Fast Track label. No filing for approval of zimislecel is mentioned, and no new timeline for it is given.

Vertex quarterly report for the quarter to 2026-09-30, filed with the United States securities regulator: the same statement in the company's own filing; the type 1 diabetes section now describes only VX-017.

Registry entry NCT04786262 (the Vertex trial; its title now reads "VX-880 and VX-017"): recruiting, 57 people planned, main results expected 2027-12-31, last updated 2026-09-01. Not changed in the window; no results posted.

Older fact the record lacks. Sumitomo Pharma release, "Announcement on the Approval for Manufacturing and Marketing Authorization of the Allogeneic iPS Cell-Derived Dopaminergic Neural Progenitor Cell Product AMCHEPRY in Japan": a conditional and time-limited approval from Japan's health ministry for improving movement symptoms in Parkinson's disease not controlled by existing drugs, based on the Kyoto University Hospital study of seven patients published in Nature in 2025. A further study after approval is required for full approval. The regulator's own list is a PDF that could not be read here.

Press report of the same decision (AFP, carried by The Star): Japan approved Amchepry for Parkinson's and a heart muscle sheet product for heart failure the same day; the Parkinson's approval described as a provisional licence resting on seven patients, four of whom improved.

Press report (Euronews, Spanish edition), one day before the window: Sumitomo Pharma reported the first transplant of Amchepry since approval, done in October 2026 at Kyoto University Hospital, with 20 to 30 patients planned by March 2029. The company's own notice was not found.

Registry entry NCT06944522, the late-stage trial of bemdaneprocel in Parkinson's disease (BlueRock Therapeutics), updated: recruiting, 102 people planned, started 2025-06-17, main results expected 2028-10. The record's estimate says this therapy is "due to read out in 2027"; the registry now says October 2028.

New registry entry NCT07911670 posted: an early trial of UX-DA003, a stem-cell-grown dopamine cell product, in 12 people with Parkinson's disease at the First Affiliated Hospital of Anhui Medical University, start expected 2026-11-23. A companion entry from the maker, Shanghai UniXell Biotechnology (NCT07733349, phase 1/2, 12 people, started 2026-09-24), was updated 2026-11-04.

Sana Biotechnology third-quarter 2026 release (filed copy): it expects to file for permission and begin a first trial of SC451, islet cells grown from stem cells and altered to hide from the immune system, "as early as this year", and reports 14-month results in one person given altered donor islets (UP421) with no anti-rejection drugs, published as a letter in the New England Journal of Medicine (DOI 10.1056/NEJMc2604408; letter not opened, date not checked). The 14-month result is donor cells, not cells grown from stem cells, so it does not count under this test; it bears on the anti-rejection drug problem the notes name.

records.estimate_direction: Two ways at once. Vertex setting zimislecel aside for a product still in its first trial moves the diabetes route later than the 2030 earliest and 2032 likely years assume, and the Parkinson's late-stage trial the estimate leans on now lists its main results for October 2028, not 2027. Against that, Japan's conditional approval of a Parkinson's cell therapy on 2026-03-06 means the clinic rung may already have been reached, which would make the whole range moot if the author counts it.
records.story_why: The record's description is built around the Vertex diabetes therapy and its expected filing; the company has now said in its own filing that it is putting its effort into a different product. A reader of this page would expect that, and would also expect the Japanese approval of 2026-03-06, which the records do not mention anywhere.

records.found: Nothing dated 2026-11-02 to 2026-11-09 was found: no registry change, no paper, no release. But the record lacks three older facts. On 2026-03-06 Japan's health ministry gave a conditional, time-limited approval to RiHEART (written ReHeart in most press), sheets of heart muscle cells grown from donor stem cells and placed on the heart, for severe heart failure after loss of blood supply (Cuorips, an Osaka University spin-off); the first use under that approval was on 2026-09-29. And on 2026-08-19 Nature Medicine published a randomised trial in 20 people of injected stem-cell-grown heart muscle cells. The author should rule on whether the Japanese approval meets the clinic rung ("a regulator approves such a graft for heart failure").

findings.what: Cuorips release, "World's First iPSC-Derived Cardiomyocyte Therapy for Heart Failure Receives Conditional Approval in Japan": conditional and time-limited marketing approval from Japan's Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare for people with "severe ischemic heart failure who have exhausted conventional treatment options"; further study after approval is required. The release gives no trial numbers; a Japan Science and Technology Agency article of 2026-05-18 says eight patients were treated in the trial and that effectiveness must be confirmed within a seven-year approval period. Two points for the author: the approval is conditional, and press reports describe the sheets as working by helping new blood vessels form, which is not the same claim as grafted muscle surviving.

Japan Science and Technology Agency article on the two approvals of 2026-03-06: both conditional and time-limited; RiHEART trial of eight patients, all with reduced symptoms and improved heart function; an expert panel had agreed on 2026-02-19.

Cuorips notice, "Notice regarding the First Transplantation of Regenerative Medicine Product RiHEART": first transplant under the approval on 2026-09-29 at Osaka Police Hospital; covered by public health insurance from 2026-09-01. A press report of 2026-10-22 (The Standard, Hong Kong) says the patient, a woman in her fifties, was recovering and due to leave hospital.

Peer-reviewed trial report in Nature Medicine (Zhang, Menasche, Wang and colleagues), the HEAL-CHF trial, registry number NCT03763136: 20 people with advanced heart failure having bypass surgery, randomised to injections of stem-cell-grown heart muscle cells or none. No lasting dangerous heart rhythm and no tumours at 12 months; every treated patient had early rhythm disturbances and two needed treatment for a fast rhythm; walking distance, blood flow and wall thickening were better than with surgery alone, but pumping (ejection fraction) was not different at 12 months. The first comparison-group result for this kind of treatment, and a mixed one. Abstract read; full text not opened.

Registry entry NCT04396899, the Göttingen patch trial the record follows: recruiting, 53 people planned, main results expected 2027-12, last updated 2026-02-20. Unchanged in the window; no results posted.

unmatched.what: Sana Biotechnology's quarterly release reports 14-month survival and working of donor insulin-making cells, altered to hide from the immune system, in one person with type 1 diabetes taking no anti-rejection drugs, and cites a letter in the New England Journal of Medicine (DOI 10.1056/NEJMc2604408; the letter itself was not opened and its date not checked).
unmatched.why_it_matters: The site's stem cell record calls the need for anti-rejection drugs the catch for ageing. These are donor cells, not cells grown from stem cells, so the result fits no record as written, but it is the first sign in a person that the drugs might be avoided.

unmatched.what: Registry entry NCT06907329, a trial of slow-release nicotinamide mononucleotide tablets on immune ageing and metabolism in middle-aged and older people, updated and listed as completed. Seen in the registry's dated list only; the entry itself was not opened and no results are posted.
unmatched.why_it_matters: Belongs to the site's record on supplements that raise NAD, which is not in this packet; a completed trial may report soon.

unmatched.what: Humacyte release on a first trial in people of its lab-grown blood vessel for heart bypass surgery, tied to the American Heart Association meeting. Seen in search results only.
unmatched.why_it_matters: A grown replacement part for a common disease of old age; the lab-grown organ record leaves blood vessels out by its own definition, so it fits nowhere.
